title: The IPv4 Header
summary: A field-by-field tour of the IPv4 header: version, IHL, DSCP, ECN, total length, fragmentation fields, TTL, protocol, checksum, and the address fields.

content.body:
Data moves down the stack by being wrapped in successive headers — **encapsulation**:

1. Upper-layer data is wrapped in a **Layer 4 header** (TCP or UDP) → a **segment**.
2. The segment is wrapped in a **Layer 3 header** (IP) → a **packet**.
3. The packet is wrapped in a **Layer 2 header and trailer** → a **frame**.

These wrapped units are called **PDUs** (protocol data units): the Layer 3 PDU is a packet, the Layer 2 PDU is a frame.

The IPv4 header holds the information routers need to route a packet to its destination. This lesson examines each field.

**Version (4 bits)** — identifies the IP version. IPv4 has a value of `4` (`0100` in binary); IPv6 has `6` (`0110`). The never-deployed Internet Stream Protocol was `5` — the "lost IPv5". In an IPv4 header this field is always 4.

**IHL — Internet Header Length (4 bits)** — the total length of the header, in **4-byte increments** (not single bytes).

- Minimum value `5` → 5 × 4 = **20 bytes** (a header with no options).
- Maximum value `15` → 15 × 4 = **60 bytes**.

So the optional options field can be at most 60 − 20 = **40 bytes**.

**DSCP — Differentiated Services Code Point (6 bits)** — used for **QoS (Quality of Service)** to prioritize delay-sensitive traffic like voice and video over best-effort traffic like a web page load.

**ECN — Explicit Congestion Notification (2 bits)** — provides end-to-end notification of network congestion *without dropping packets*. Normally congestion is signaled by dropping packets; ECN flags it instead. It requires both endpoints and the network infrastructure to support it.

**Total Length (16 bits)** — the length of the entire packet (IPv4 header + encapsulated Layer 4 segment) in **bytes**. Unlike IHL, this counts single bytes.

- Minimum value 20 (a bare 20-byte header with no data).
- Maximum value **65,535** (the maximum 16-bit value: 128 + 64 + … + 32,768).

It's different from IHL, which measures only the header.

A packet larger than the **MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit)** — usually **1500 bytes**, matching Ethernet's maximum payload — must be **fragmented**. Fragments are reassembled by the **receiving host**.

- **Identification (16 bits)** — all fragments of the same original packet share this value, so they can be reassembled.
- **Flags (3 bits)** — bit 0 is reserved (always 0); bit 1 is the **DF (Don't Fragment)** bit — set to 1 to prevent fragmentation; bit 2 is the **MF (More Fragments)** bit — 1 on every fragment except the last.
- **Fragment Offset (13 bits)** — the position of the fragment within the original packet, so fragments can be reassembled even if they arrive out of order.

**Time to Live (8 bits)** — prevents packets from looping forever. Each router decrements the TTL by one; when it reaches **0, the router drops the packet**.

Originally designed to represent a packet's lifetime in seconds, in practice it is a **hop count**. The recommended default TTL is **64** (the maximum value is 255).

**Protocol (8 bits)** — identifies the encapsulated Layer 4 protocol. Key values to remember:

| Value | Protocol |
|---|---|
| 1 | ICMP (ping) |
| 6 | TCP |
| 17 | UDP |
| 89 | OSPF |

**Header Checksum (16 bits)** — a calculated checksum used to detect errors **in the IPv4 header only**. If a router's recalculated checksum doesn't match, it drops the packet. Errors in the *encapsulated data* are the responsibility of the Layer 4 protocol (TCP/UDP checksums) — IP does not check them.

**Source IP Address (32 bits)** — the sender's IPv4 address.

**Destination IP Address (32 bits)** — the intended receiver's IPv4 address.

**Options** — an optional, variable-length field (0 to 320 bits / 40 bytes), rarely used. If **IHL is greater than 5**, options are present. For CCNA purposes, you don't need to memorize the options structure.

content.body:
In a Wireshark capture of a ping between two routers, the IPv4 header for a 100-byte ping shows:

- **Version** 4, **Header Length** 5 (20 bytes).
- **Total Length** 100 bytes, **Identification** a small value, **TTL** 255, **Protocol** ICMP (1).

A ping forced larger than the MTU (`ping 192.168.1.2 size 10000`) gets fragmented into 1500-byte fragments: each has the same **Identification** value, the **More Fragments** bit set except on the last fragment, and increasing **Fragment Offset** values. Setting the **DF bit** on a packet larger than the MTU makes the ping **fail** — it can't be sent whole and isn't allowed to fragment.

High-yield facts: the IPv4 **version field is always 4 (0100)**; **TTL** reaching 0 drops the packet; the **header checksum** checks only the header — the encapsulated protocol (TCP/UDP) checks the data; the **options** field is the only variable-length field; and the **MF (More Fragments)** bit is set on every fragment except the last.

questions.question: What is the fixed binary value of the first field of an IPv4 header?
questions.explanation: The first field is the version field. For an IPv4 header it is always 4, which is 0100 in binary.

questions.question: Which IPv4 header field will cause the packet to be dropped if it has a value of zero?
questions.explanation: TTL (Time to Live) is decremented by one at each router. When it reaches zero, the packet is dropped. DSCP, IHL, and ECN do not cause dropping at zero.

questions.question: How are errors in an IPv4 packet's encapsulated data detected?
questions.explanation: The IPv4 header checksum only checks the IPv4 header itself. The encapsulated Layer 4 protocol (TCP or UDP) uses its own checksum to check for errors in the data.

options.label: A
options.text: The IPv4 header checksum checks for errors in the data

options.label: B
options.text: The encapsulated protocol (e.g. TCP or UDP) checks for errors

options.label: C
options.text: Errors in the encapsulated data cannot be detected

questions.question: Which field of the IPv4 header is variable in length?
questions.explanation: The options field can vary from 0 bits up to 320 bits (40 bytes). All other fields are fixed length — although IHL and total length represent variable lengths, the fields themselves are fixed.

questions.question: Which bit will be set to 1 on all IPv4 packet fragments except the last fragment?
questions.explanation: The More Fragments (MF) bit, part of the flags field, indicates the current fragment is not the last. It is 1 on all fragments except the last, which sets it to 0.
